title: A straight line on a 1000/T plot is an activation energy
summary: Reaction rates and ignition delays change by orders of magnitude with temperature. Plot the logarithm against 1000/T and an Arrhenius process becomes a straight line whose slope is the activation energy.

media.alt: Semi-log plot of ignition delay against 1000/T for three equivalence ratios. Markers are synthetic experiments, lines are a model; all three series fall on nearly straight lines that run from the lower left to the upper right.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F9.1 with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery), not a project result.

source.note: Standard physical chemistry. The figure is the design system's synthetic F9.1 render, so no project number is quoted.

read_the_figure.question: Does the model reproduce the measured ignition delay across temperature, and what apparent activation energy does each series have?
read_the_figure.axes: x: 1000/T in 1/K, so hot is on the left and cold on the right. y: ignition delay on a logarithmic scale, so equal vertical steps are equal factors.
look_at: Markers are experiments, lines are the model, one colour per equivalence ratio.
Straightness: a straight series is one Arrhenius-like process; curvature means the controlling chemistry changes with temperature.
Slope: a steeper line means a larger apparent activation energy, so a stronger temperature dependence.
Vertical offset between lines at the same x is a ratio, not a difference: one decade apart means ten times.
read_the_figure.proves: Markers scattering evenly around the line over the whole x range is evidence that the model captures the temperature dependence of the controlling step.
if_wrong: Markers drifting systematically away from the line at one end: the model's effective activation energy is off there.

A bend or S-shape in the data: competing chemistry (for fuels with a negative temperature coefficient region, delay can even stop falling with temperature) which a single straight line cannot describe.
A plot against T instead of 1/T: the curve is strongly bent and the slope tells you nothing directly.
must_check: Experiment markers visibly distinct from model lines.
Pressure and composition stated for every series.
Units of 1000/T given as 1/K, and a temperature axis on top if the audience thinks in kelvin.

terms.meaning: The factor k that multiplies concentrations in a rate law, rate = k [A][B]. It carries all the temperature dependence.
The rate at infinite temperature: the collision frequency times geometry factors. Units follow the reaction order.
The energy barrier, per mole, that molecules must climb for the reaction to proceed. Large barrier, strong temperature dependence.
8.314 J per mole per kelvin. It converts the barrier per mole into the dimensionless ratio E_a / RT.
The fraction of molecules with enough energy to cross the barrier: the exponential in the rate law.
The time from the start of a constant-condition experiment until the mixture ignites, usually defined by a temperature rise or a radical peak.
The energy obtained by treating a many-step process as if it were one Arrhenius step: the fitted slope of ln tau against 1/T.
Fuel-to-oxidiser ratio relative to the exact stoichiometric ratio; 1 is stoichiometric, below 1 lean, above 1 rich.

remember: Take logs: ln k is linear in 1/T, with slope -E_a / R and intercept ln A.
On a 1000/T axis, E_a = -1000 R times the slope of ln k (or +1000 R times the slope of ln tau).
Hot is left, cold is right on a 1/T axis. Steeper means more temperature-sensitive.
A straight line is the assumption of one dominant step. Curvature is information.

steps.title: The rate law
steps.note: Arrhenius (1889); collision theory explains A as a collision rate and the exponential as the fraction of collisions with enough energy (Trautz 1916, Lewis 1918).

steps.title: Take the logarithm
steps.note: In the variable 1/T this is a straight line. Verified symbolically: the derivative of ln k with respect to 1/T is -E_a / R.

steps.title: Rescale the axis to 1000/T
steps.note: 1/T is around 0.001 per kelvin, awkward to read. Multiplying by 1000 puts the ticks at 0.8, 1.0, 1.2 and leaves the slope easy to convert.

steps.title: Compare two temperatures without the constant A
steps.note: A cancels, so one ratio of measurements gives E_a, and one E_a predicts a ratio.

steps.title: A decade on the axis
steps.note: For E_a = 150 kJ/mol this is about 0.128: the horizontal distance over which k changes by a factor ten. Useful for judging a slope by eye.

steps.title: From a rate to an ignition delay
steps.note: Ignition is a chain of steps, but near a single controlling step the delay behaves like 1/k. The slope is now positive (hot means shorter), and E_eff is only an apparent energy.

steps.title: Where the straight line fails
steps.tex: \frac{d\ln\tau}{d(1000/T)}=\frac{E_\mathrm{eff}(T)}{1000\,R}\quad\text{(a function of }T\text{ when the plot bends)}
steps.note: If the controlling chemistry changes with temperature the slope itself changes: the plot bends. Some fuels even show a region where the delay stops falling as T rises, which no single Arrhenius line can follow.

worked.title: How much faster is a reaction at 1200 K than at 1000 K?
worked.problem: Take E_a = 150 kJ/mol. By what factor does k increase from 1000 K to 1200 K?
worked.answer: A factor of about 20: a 20 percent rise in temperature gives a twenty-fold rate.

analyze.q: In the reference plot the three lines are almost parallel. What does that say about how equivalence ratio enters the model, and what would you expect to see if it changed the controlling step?
analyze.hint: Parallel lines mean equal slope; a vertical shift is a constant ratio.

analyze.q: A series of data points is concave on a 1000/T plot. Give two physical explanations and one measurement artefact that could produce the same shape.
analyze.hint: Changing controlling step, competing channels; non-uniform temperature in the apparatus.

analyze.q: Why does a plot of tau against T (not 1/T) hide the Arrhenius structure even on a log axis?

evaluate.q: A group fits E_eff to six points between 1000 and 1100 K and quotes 120 kJ/mol; another fits a different set over 800 to 1250 K and quotes 180. Which result do you trust more, and what would make them comparable?
evaluate.hint: Standard error of a slope grows when the x range shrinks; the apparent energy can change with T.

evaluate.q: Is a model 'validated' because its line runs through the markers on this plot? What else would you ask for?
evaluate.hint: Other pressures, other compositions, quantified scatter and a residual plot.

create: Design the same figure for a fuel that shows a negative-temperature-coefficient region: what axis ranges, markers and annotations would let a reader see the region without reading the legend?
Add a secondary axis along the top that shows temperature in kelvin. Which tick values would you choose for 1000/T between 0.7 and 1.5, and why?

checks.q: Why plot against 1/T rather than T?
checks.hint: What does ln k look like as a function of T, and as a function of 1/T?
checks.answer: Because ln k = ln A - (E_a/R)(1/T) is exactly linear in 1/T but not in T. A straight line makes the slope readable as an energy and makes departures from the one-step picture obvious.

checks.q: The slope of ln k against 1000/T is -12.0. What is the activation energy?
checks.answer: E_a = 1000 x 8.314 x 12.0 = 99.8 kJ/mol, about 100 kJ/mol.

checks.q: On a 1000/T plot, data fall on a line that gets steeper toward the cold end. What does that say about the controlling step?
checks.answer: The apparent activation energy increases as temperature falls: a step with a higher barrier takes control at low temperature, or the mixture moves from one chemical regime to another. A single Arrhenius step would give a constant slope.

checks.q: Two experiments agree on the slope but one has a tenfold larger intercept. What does that mean physically, and how would you decide whether it is real?
checks.hint: Intercept is ln A (or ln B).
checks.answer: The pre-exponential factor differs by a factor of ten: same temperature sensitivity, different absolute speed. It can be real (different concentrations or pressure) or an artefact (different delay definition, calibration). Check the pressure and composition of both, the definition of ignition and repeat runs before believing it.

checks.q: You have three measured ignition delays at 900, 1000 and 1100 K. How do you estimate E_eff and say how uncertain it is?
checks.hint: Linear regression of ln tau on 1000/T.
checks.answer: Compute x = 1000/T, regress ln tau on x, and take E_eff = 1000 R times the slope. The standard error of the slope (from the residuals and the spread of x) gives the uncertainty. With three points that interval is wide, which is itself the message: measure over a longer temperature range.
